description: Frantic Assembly, Complicite and the storytelling traditions a director borrows to stage Verne.
content_html:
Why Practitioners Matter for This Play

When examiners ask students to apply a practitioner’s techniques to a set play, they are not asking for a biography. They want to see students understand how a specific working method — a way of creating scenes, rehearsing the ensemble, constructing images or relating to the audience — could shape the choices a modern company makes when staging this text. For Around the World in 80 Days, three practitioner traditions are directly relevant and practically applicable: Frantic Assembly, Complicite, and the music-hall and circus tradition that the play’s comic form echoes.

Key Fact

The three most relevant practitioner traditions are: Frantic Assembly (ensemble physical theatre, contact work, collaborative image-making), Complicite (object transformation, storytelling ensemble, narrator-led staging) and the music-hall/circus tradition (direct audience address, comic precision, shared theatrical pleasure).

Frantic Assembly: Bodies as Storytelling Instruments

Frantic Assembly, founded by Scott Graham and Steven Hoggett in 1994, built its reputation on a form of physical theatre in which the body is not decorative but dramaturgical — the body’s movement tells the story and creates the emotional world of the play. Their signature vocabulary includes round-by-through exercises, chair duets and contact choreography, and lifts that serve narrative rather than spectacle.

In Around the World in 80 Days, Frantic Assembly’s influence is most visible in the sequences where the company must become a single creature or vehicle. The elephant sequence, the train sequence, the ship — all require the same principle Frantic Assembly built their method on: the whole is more than the sum of its parts, and the audience reads a collective physical decision as a single image. A director working from Frantic Assembly’s approach would develop these sequences in rehearsal through physical improvisation, allowing the company to find the movement together rather than having it choreographed from outside.

As a performer working in a Frantic Assembly-influenced rehearsal for the elephant sequence, you might begin the devising process with a round-by-through exercise in which two performers in physical contact with each other explore the rhythm and weight of a large, slow-moving creature. The goal is not to mime an elephant — it is to find the weight and rhythm in your own body so the physical choice becomes instinctive. Your vocal contribution in this scene is silence: the physical precision carries the full dramatic load.

As a lighting designer for a Frantic Assembly-influenced staging of this sequence, you would trust the physical storytelling and resist the temptation to overilluminate. A warm amber wash from a high angle (suggesting the Indian sun), perhaps a dim state with a gobo of leaf-shadow patterns projected onto the floor — giving the ensemble’s bodies maximum visual impact against a subtly textured background — would be the Frantic Assembly aesthetic: clean, powerful, serving the movement without competing with it.

Complicite: Object Transformation and the Narrator

Complicite (founded 1983, still directed by Simon McBurney) built a different but equally relevant tradition. Where Frantic Assembly’s strength is in the physical ensemble, Complicite’s signature is in object transformation and in the figure of the storytelling narrator. In Complicite’s productions, company members regularly step in and out of the fiction to address the audience directly, to handle and transform objects, and to remind the audience that they are watching a story being told, not a reality being reproduced.

This is exactly the theatrical mode Eason’s script requires. The Complicite-influenced director would pay close attention to the way objects change meaning during the play: a chair is never just a chair once the ensemble has trained itself to use it as a carriage; a rope is never just a rope once it has been ship rigging. The discipline is that the transformation must be total and committed — there is no half-way position where the audience is uncertain whether this is a chair or a carriage. Complicite’s training method emphasises that the object’s transformation is effected entirely by the performer’s physical relationship to it.

Key Fact

Complicite’s core principle: the object’s meaning is entirely created by the performer’s physical use of it. A chair becomes a train carriage the moment the performer sits in it as if in a moving carriage — not because the chair looks like a carriage, but because the body’s logic makes it one.

Brechtian Elements: The Narrator and the Episodic Frame

Bertolt Brecht’s theatrical principles also have limited but specific relevance here. Brecht’s Verfremdungseffekt (alienation effect) — using narration, direct address and visible theatricality to remind the audience they are watching a construction — is built into Eason’s structure. Every time a company member steps forward to narrate the passage of days or comment on Fogg’s progress, they perform a Brechtian function: the story is held at arm’s length so the audience can observe it.

The episodic structure — short scenes in clearly labelled locations, no attempt at continuous realistic time — is also Brechtian in spirit. Brecht’s epic theatre avoided the seamless illusion of naturalism in favour of a structure that acknowledged each scene as a discrete unit. However, important to note: Around the World in 80 Days is not a Brechtian play in the full sense — it does not make political-didactic demands on its audience in the way The Caucasian Chalk Circle does. The Brechtian elements are structural tools within a comedy-of-adventure, not an ideological programme.

Victorian music hall — the variety entertainment tradition that was the dominant popular theatre form when Verne’s novel was published — operated on principles that resonate strongly with Eason’s play. Direct audience address was the norm; performers acknowledged the presence of the audience and played to them explicitly. Comic precision — the exact timing of a pratfall, the perfectly judged pause before a punchline — was a highly valued craft skill. Songs, physical spectacle, and an awareness that the audience’s pleasure was the goal rather than their passive observation were all central.

Some productions of this play interpolate live music — a piano onstage, a percussionist tracking the journey — that explicitly invokes this tradition. A director drawing on music-hall principles would coach Passepartout in particular on the shared, audience-aware quality of his comedy: the moment when he turns to the audience with an expression of disbelief, or when he makes an aside directly to the front row, is the music-hall gesture surviving into 21st-century ensemble theatre. In terms of performer-audience relationship, this play operates much closer to the music-hall end of the spectrum than to the fourth-wall naturalism of Stanislavski.
exam_tip_html: When applying a practitioner to a set play, the most common error is to describe the practitioner’s biography or general philosophy without showing how a specific technique applies to a specific moment of the play. The examiner wants you to say: “Using Frantic Assembly’s contact choreography approach, the director would develop the elephant sequence through physical improvisation in rehearsal, allowing the ensemble to find a shared weight and rhythm that makes the creature credible — the physical logic of the movement, not a visual representation, persuades the audience.” That is a practitioner applied to a moment. Compare: “Frantic Assembly like physical theatre” — that is biography, not application. For the 8-mark questions in this lesson, make sure your performer or designer response also demonstrates how the practitioner’s principles shape the specific choices you make.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Frantic Assembly’s ensemble physical theatre tradition — collaborative devising, contact choreography, bodies-as-storytelling-instruments — is directly applicable to the play’s most demanding ensemble sequences (the elephant, the train, the ship).
  • Complicite’s object transformation principle (an object’s meaning is created entirely by the performer’s physical use of it) and its narrator-led storytelling mode are built into the structure Eason has written.
  • The music-hall tradition, with its direct audience address, comic precision and shared theatrical pleasure, explains the quality of the performer-audience relationship the play requires — far from Stanislavskian fourth-wall naturalism.

practice_questions.text: Name one physical theatre company whose ensemble methods are directly relevant to staging Around the World in 80 Days.
Define the term 'Verfremdungseffekt' as it applies to theatrical performance.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that Verfremdungseffekt (alienation effect) is a technique associated with Brecht; 1 mark for explaining that it involves reminding the audience they are watching a theatrical construction, preventing passive emotional identification and encouraging critical thinking.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Complicite's principle of object transformation could be applied to the scene in which chairs become a railway carriage. What must the performers do for the transformation to be successful?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identifying Complicite's principle that object transformation is achieved through the performer's physical relationship to the object, not through the object's appearance (1); describing specific physical choices the performer must make (the sway of a moving carriage, holding an imaginary armrest, gaze from an invisible window) (1); explaining what happens if the commitment breaks (the fiction collapses, the audience loses the transformation) (1); explaining the effect on the audience when it succeeds (collective reading of the chairs as carriage through the performers' physical logic) (1).

practice_questions.text: As a performer working in a Frantic Assembly-influenced rehearsal for the train attack sequence, explain the vocal and physical choices you would make to play an ensemble member caught in the chaos. Refer to Frantic Assembly's working methods and to specific performer choices for this moment.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Both vocal AND physical choices specific and named, anchored to the train attack sequence. Physical: reference to Frantic Assembly's contact choreography principles (bodies reacting to each other's physical initiatives); specific physical choices for the chaos (disorganised centre of gravity, low levels — crouching or falling — contrasting with the earlier organised train rows); how the body communicates fear or urgency without overacting (specific postural choice, e.g. pulling arms in, chin down, rapid weight transfer). Vocal: how voice changes under duress (increased pace, shorter phrases, possibly fragmented syntax); reference to the silence of mime sections. Both choices justified with named effect on the audience. The Frantic Assembly context is applied to a specific moment, not just described in general.

Secure: At least one vocal and one physical choice named, both anchored to the train attack. Frantic Assembly is referenced meaningfully. Some audience effect stated.

Developing: Describes the chaos of the scene physically but without specific choices or Frantic Assembly methodology. Effects implied.

Emerging: Describes what happens in the scene without any performer choices or practitioner reference.

practice_questions.text: As a lighting and sound designer working from Complicite's aesthetic principles, explain how you would design the Atlantic crossing scene. Refer to how your design choices support the company's physical storytelling rather than competing with it.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific lighting choices that serve the physical storytelling (not competing with it): a minimal, clean wash (Complicite’s aesthetic is rarely overlit); named lantern choices; a specific gobo or effect for the ocean surface; transitions that respond to the physical action rather than leading it. Sound: a specific soundscape that enhances the physical vocabulary (creaking timbers, water sound built from below); how the non-diegetic underscore supports the physical rhythm of the ensemble rather than overriding it; named instruments or textures. Every choice is justified as serving the physical storytelling. Named effect on the audience.

Secure: At least two named design elements (one lighting, one sound) with effects, and at least one is connected to supporting rather than competing with the physical work.

Developing: Design choices are present but the connection to Complicite's principles is not made. Generic descriptions.

Emerging: Basic listing of design ideas with no practitioner context.

practice_questions.text: As a director drawing on the traditions of Frantic Assembly, Complicite and the music-hall form, explain how you would stage the opening Reform Club scene and the moment the wager is made. Cover your approach to performer direction, staging configuration, lighting, sound and the performer-audience relationship.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full directorial vision drawing coherently on the three practitioner traditions. Frantic Assembly: the physical precision of the Reform Club ensemble — how the company moves as a social unit (shared weight, status physicality, a Frantic Assembly-devised movement score for the club's rituals). Complicite: the narrator stepping forward to address the audience; objects already becoming symbols (the chairs as club furniture, the pocket watch as the play's central image). Music hall: the awareness of the audience's presence even in this early scene; perhaps a direct address to the front row at the moment the wager is proposed, recruiting the audience as judge. Staging configuration: the choice of formation for the Reform Club (upstage semicircle with Fogg downstage, OR a cluster with Fogg central); the lighting state (precise, formal, slightly cold for London precision); sound (a clock ticking, perhaps a distant locomotive whistle as the wager is made, foreshadowing). The performer-audience relationship is explicitly addressed. Every choice has a named effect. A directorial statement about the overall intended experience.

Secure: Most disciplines covered, with at least two of the three practitioner traditions meaningfully applied. Concrete choices. Some audience effect.

Developing: Some disciplines covered; practitioner references are general rather than specific to the moment. Effects implied.

Emerging: Basic description of the scene with little practitioner application or design specifics.

knowledge_checks.q: Which theatre company is known for object transformation and narrator-led ensemble storytelling?
What does Brecht's Verfremdungseffekt aim to prevent in the audience?
options: Passive emotional identification — it encourages critical thinking instead
The use of direct address by performers

knowledge_checks.q: Frantic Assembly was founded in _____ by Scott Graham and Steven Hoggett.
In Complicite's method, a chair becomes a train carriage through the performer's _____ relationship to the object, not through its appearance.
Match each practitioner tradition to its most relevant technique for this play.
right: Contact choreography and ensemble bodies creating shared physical images
Direct audience address, comic precision and shared theatrical pleasure

flashcard_questions.q: When was Frantic Assembly founded, and by whom?
flashcard_questions.a: 1994, by Scott Graham and Steven Hoggett.

flashcard_questions.q: When was Complicite founded, and by whom?
What is Frantic Assembly's main working method?
flashcard_questions.a: Collaborative physical devising, contact choreography and ensemble bodies as storytelling instruments.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Complicite's core principle of object transformation?
flashcard_questions.a: An object's meaning is created by the performer's physical use of it, not its appearance.
Brecht's alienation effect: techniques to prevent passive identification and encourage critical thinking.

flashcard_questions.q: What is round-by-through in Frantic Assembly's method?
flashcard_questions.a: An exercise where performers take turns responding to each other's physical initiation, building shared movement.
Whether the audience is a passive observer or an active participant in the theatrical event.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the music-hall tradition's key performance quality?
flashcard_questions.a: Direct audience address, comic precision and shared theatrical pleasure.

flashcard_questions.q: What Brechtian element is built into Eason's script structure?
flashcard_questions.a: Narrator direct address and episodic scene structure that acknowledges the theatrical construction.
Using a prop to represent multiple different things, the change achieved by the performer's physical use.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a dim state in lighting design?
flashcard_questions.a: A lighting state in which the intensity is reduced to a very low level, creating shadow and mystery.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is Around the World in 80 Days not a fully Brechtian play?
flashcard_questions.a: It uses Brechtian structural tools within a comedy-of-adventure, not as an ideological political programme.

glossary_terms.definition: A physical theatre company founded in 1994 by Scott Graham and Steven Hoggett, known for high-energy ensemble work, lifts, contact choreography and collaboratively devised movement.
A theatre company founded by Simon McBurney in 1983, known for object transformation, storytelling ensemble work, narrator-led staging and precise physical imagery.
A comic performance tradition, particularly popular in Victorian-era variety entertainment, that emphasises direct audience address, comic precision, timing, song and shared theatrical pleasure.
A choreographic method developed by Frantic Assembly in which pairs of performers create movement by taking turns to respond to each other's physical initiation, building shared physical language.
Contact work in which performers manipulate, support or move each other's bodies, creating images that could not be achieved alone and communicating vulnerability, trust or power.

The theatrical technique of using a prop or simple object to represent multiple things during a performance, the transformation happening through the performer's physical use of the object rather than through its appearance.
Brecht's term for a suite of theatrical techniques designed to prevent the audience from losing themselves in the drama, encouraging critical thinking instead of passive emotional identification.
The quality of movement, particularly its relationship to the ground, often described in terms of how light or heavy a performer's steps and gestures feel.
The relationship between performers and audience, including whether the audience is positioned as passive observers or active participants in the theatrical event.
A lighting state in which the intensity is reduced to a very low level, creating shadow and mystery.
